newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Sofia mayor is Bulgaria's caretaker premier.
newsitem.headline: Sofia mayor is Bulgaria's caretaker premier.

text.p: Sofia's respected opposition mayor Stefan Sofianski , sworn in on Wednesday to head an interim cabinet until after elections in April, immediately warned Bulgarians he could offer no smooth ride out of economic chaos.

"At the moment the country is in severe economic crisis, from which we can escape only at the price of many efforts, not only from one person and one cabinet but from all of us," Sofianski told reporters after the swearing-in ceremony.
"It is very important that during those months we put aside our small conflicts and mobilise all patience and decisiveness," he said.
He said the first big step had been taken with an all-party declaration on principles for the interim cabinet's handling of the crisis, signed by political leaders on Tuesday.
"Our ambition is to make the second step through reasonable behaviour and government with a human face," he said.

Sofianski told Reuters in an interview last Friday a month-long campaign to remove the Socialists from power had given Bulgarians new motivation and he was hopeful that Bulgaria could now catch up with other ex-communist states.

The ex-communist Socialists won elections in December 1994 but lost the confidence of the electorate because of their government's corruption and failure to carry out reforms agreed with international lenders.

"Unfortunately, maybe as a nation, maybe as a parliament or a government, we have not succeeded in passing through this transition period, and unfortunately, if we look behind, we see nobody behind us in terms of reform," Sofianski said.

"The last years have been especially bad for the country, with a lot of problems in the government, in parliament, a lot of corruption at high levels of government, and that makes the transition period very difficult."
An economist by training, Sofianski was elected mayor in November 1995. He has said he will return to the municipality after the April 19 general election to complete his term.

His ability to keep the city running smoothly despite deep economic crisis has won him the respect of residents. Last year he visited Moscow to negotiate a barter deal exchanging goods for Russian crude to ensure winter fuel supplies.
When opposition protesters besieged and ransacked parliament on January 10, Sofianski played a prominent role trying to calm tension inside and outside parliament.
The next day, municipality staff and opposition supporters worked together to clean up the debris, clearing wrecked cars and mending smashed windows to remove all traces of the riot.

Sofianski, 45, is married with three daughters. His wife is often seen with him at public functions or in Sofia's jazz clubs, and the whole family took part in his 1995 election campaign. He is famous for his smiling, affable manner and widely liked by his staff.
Sofianski is a senior member of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces, currently favourite to win the elections, which he expects to mark a sea change in Bulgarian politics.
"People had no motivation, they have it now," he said.
"Now people at least have a certain hope for change. The hope is that there will be no more people like the former communists in the government of the country."
